error_modes.label: DEVIATION FROM TURNING POINTS (radius)
error_modes.source: specific:DEVIATION FROM TURNING POINTS* (radius in NM)

texts.0: SP, due to map reading based on a single ground feature instead of a pattern of features, did not overfly the turning points within the required radius. SP passed the second turning point about 4 NM abeam and the third about 5 NM abeam, well beyond the 2 NM radius, and the ground track diverged progressively from the planned leg. IP had to take over the navigation and direct SP back onto the planned track before the next leg could be flown.
texts.1: SP, due to an early acceptance of a road junction that resembled the briefed feature, did not overfly the turning points within the tighter radius. SP passed the turning points about 2 NM abeam, at the outer limit of the standard, and repositioned onto the planned track only after IP pointed out the correct feature over the intercom. Each subsequent turning point required the same verbal prompting to keep the deviation from growing further.
texts.2: SP, due to a heading held without allowance for the reported wind on the first leg, initially tracked about 1.7 NM to the right of the planned turning point. SP compared the terrain with the chart, identified the offset while still inbound and applied a correction that placed the aircraft over the following turning points inside the radius. No IP input was required at any stage of the correction.
texts.3: SP overflew every turning point within a radius of 1 NM, positively identifying each one against the chart before commencing the turn. Track corrections were small and applied early, so no leg required a repositioning maneuver. Navigation continued from each turning point without any regain of track.
texts.4: SP overflew each turning point practically overhead, with the aircraft crossing the selected features rather than passing abeam of them. Wind corrections were computed and applied on every leg, so the lateral deviation remained negligible throughout the route. Chart and terrain agreed at every point of the navigation.
texts.marginal: SP overflew the turning points within standards, but the offset was consistently on the same side of track and grew toward 1 NM by the final legs. The trend is a wind correction that is applied once at the start of the navigation and is not revised as the actual drift becomes apparent. SP is expected to reassess drift on each leg and keep the turning points overhead rather than at the edge of the acceptable radius.

texts.0: SP, due to a leg flown at an airspeed well below the planned one without any recomputation, did not arrive at the turning points at the calculated times. Arrival at the second turning point was about 2 minutes late and at the third about 2 minutes 30 seconds late, far beyond the 60 second tolerance. IP had to compute the required groundspeed and direct the power setting in order to restore the timing of the remaining legs.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed start of the leg timing after the turn was completed, arrived at the turning points about 60 seconds outside the calculated times, at the limit of the standard. SP adjusted the airspeed only after IP asked for the running time on the leg, and the same delay reappeared on the following leg. The timing was contained within the standard solely through repeated verbal prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a groundspeed check made late in the first leg, initially built an error of about 50 seconds against the calculated arrival time. SP identified the discrepancy at the midpoint of the leg, computed the required correction and adjusted the airspeed so that the following turning points were crossed within 30 seconds of the plan. No IP intervention was needed to recover the timing.
texts.3: SP arrived at each turning point within 30 seconds of the calculated time, starting and stopping the leg timing at the correct points. Groundspeed was checked early on every leg and small airspeed adjustments were applied before the error could accumulate. Timing on all turning points remained inside the tighter criterion.
texts.4: SP arrived at every turning point within a few seconds of the calculated time, with the timing error never allowed to build on any leg. Groundspeed was recomputed at each half-leg checkpoint and the airspeed corrections applied were small and anticipatory. Deviations from the planned arrival times were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP arrived at the turning points within standards, but the arrival times were consistently early and the error grew from leg to leg toward the 30 second figure. The trend is an airspeed flown above the planned one without an accompanying check of the effect on leg timing. SP is expected to check groundspeed against the plan early in each leg and to correct the airspeed while the timing error is still small.

texts.0: SP, due to timing errors on successive legs that were never corrected once identified, did not control the total duration of the navigation flight. The route was completed about 3 minutes later than the planned total time, well beyond the 90 second tolerance, and the recovery time no longer matched the flight plan. IP had to reassign the airspeed and delete a portion of the final leg in order to recover the sortie within the fuel available.
texts.1: SP, due to individual leg errors that were treated in isolation rather than against the running total, completed the navigation about 90 seconds off the planned total time, at the limit of the standard. SP began adjusting the airspeed only after IP asked for the accumulated time against the plan. The total time was kept inside the standard only because of that prompting on the last leg.
texts.2: SP, due to a slower than planned groundspeed on the first two legs, accumulated an error of about 70 seconds against the planned total time. SP recognized the accumulation while abeam the third turning point, increased the airspeed for the remaining legs and completed the navigation within 45 seconds of the plan. The correction was computed and applied without IP input.
texts.3: SP completed the navigation within 45 seconds of the planned total time, monitoring the accumulated time against the plan at each turning point. Where a leg produced a small error, SP absorbed it on the following leg rather than carrying it forward. The total duration of the flight matched the mission plan.
texts.4: SP completed the navigation within a few seconds of the planned total time, with the running total kept aligned with the plan throughout the route. Every leg error was identified at the turning point and absorbed immediately, so nothing accumulated toward the end of the navigation. The deviation on total time was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP completed the navigation within standards, but the accumulated error reached the 45 second figure and was only absorbed on the last leg. The trend is a total time that is checked at the end of the route rather than maintained at each turning point. SP is expected to compare the running total against the plan at every turning point and to spread the correction over the remaining legs.

error_modes.label: IDENTIFICATION OF TURNING POINTS AGAINST THE CHART

texts.0: SP, due to lack of awareness of the aircraft position relative to the planned route, did not recognize the turning points confidently. SP misidentified the second turning point, called a lake that was not the briefed feature and continued on a heading that belonged to a different leg. IP had to identify the correct feature, state the aircraft position and reestablish the navigation for SP.
texts.1: SP, due to lack of awareness of a terrain feature that was available in the mission planning material, recognized the turning points only with hesitation. SP overflew the feature without calling it and identified it as the turning point only after IP asked what was below the aircraft. Recognition of the remaining points continued to depend on the same prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial fixation on a single linear feature instead of the briefed pattern of features, was slow to recognize the third turning point. SP widened the visual search, cross-checked two secondary features against the chart and identified the point positively while still able to turn on the planned track. The remaining turning points were recognized without hesitation and without IP assistance.
texts.3: SP recognized all turning points confidently, identifying each one against the chart before reaching it and announcing it in good time. The visual search was based on a pattern of features rather than a single object, so no point was confused with a similar one. Navigation proceeded from each recognized point without doubt about the aircraft position.
texts.4: SP recognized every turning point well in advance, calling each feature and its confirming secondary features while still inbound on the leg. Position awareness along the route was continuous and SP was able to state the aircraft position relative to the plan at any moment. Recognition was immediate and unambiguous at every point.
texts.marginal: SP recognized the turning points within standards, but the identification was made only overhead the feature and rested on one object at a time. The trend is a visual search that starts too late to allow a confirmation before the turn. SP is expected to begin identifying the next turning point early in the leg and to confirm it with secondary features before reaching it.

error_modes.label: TIMELY TURN AND ROLLOUT ON THE NEXT HEADING

texts.0: SP, due to a turn started only after the turning point had been left well behind, did not turn to the next heading timely. SP rolled out about 20 degrees off the planned heading and did not correct it, so the following leg was flown displaced from the planned track from the start. IP had to command the corrected heading and supervise the regain of the planned track.
texts.1: SP, due to a turn commenced without the next heading having been selected in advance, turned late toward the next heading and rolled out about 12 degrees off. SP corrected the heading only after IP stated the planned figure over the intercom. The same late selection and prompted correction were repeated at the following turning point.
texts.2: SP, due to a bank angle chosen without allowance for the size of the heading change, initially rolled out about 8 degrees short of the planned heading. SP compared the heading with the planned one immediately after rollout, applied the correction within a few seconds and continued the leg on track. Subsequent turns were flown onto the planned heading without deviation and without IP input.
texts.3: SP turned to the next heading timely at each turning point, with the next heading already known before the turn was commenced. Rollout was on the planned heading and the new leg was flown on track from the outset. No heading correction was required after any of the turns.
texts.4: SP commenced each turn precisely at the turning point and rolled out exactly on the planned heading, with the bank angle selected to suit the size of every heading change. The next heading and leg time were set up before the point was reached, so the transition between legs was seamless. Heading deviations after rollout were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP turned to the next headings within standards, but the turns were commenced slightly late and the rollouts were consistently a few degrees short of the planned figure. The trend is a turn that begins as a reaction to passing the feature rather than as a planned action. SP is expected to preset the next heading and to anticipate the turn so that rollout occurs on the planned heading.

error_modes.label: TURNING POINT OBSCURED BY CLOUD - TIMED TURN

texts.0: SP, due to retention of the briefed mental model after the actual conditions had changed, did not turn to the next point at the completion of the leg time when the turning point was covered by clouds. SP continued straight ahead searching visually for the obscured feature and overflew the point by more than 3 minutes of flight. IP had to command the turn and reconstruct the remaining route timing.
texts.1: SP, due to an aircraft position that had diverged from the mental model without being reassessed, did not turn at the completion of the leg time over the cloud covered turning point. SP started the turn about 60 seconds late, after IP asked what the leg time was showing. The dependence on that prompting persisted when the following point was also obscured.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial decision to continue searching for the obscured feature through a gap in the cloud, allowed about 40 seconds to pass beyond the completion of the leg time. SP then referred to the leg timing, accepted it as the primary reference and turned onto the next heading before the error could affect the following leg. The decision and the turn were made without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP turned to the next point at the completion of the leg time whenever the turning point was covered by clouds, without waiting for a visual identification that was not available. The turn was flown onto the preplanned heading and the timing of the following leg was started correctly. Navigation continued unaffected by the cloud cover.
texts.4: SP anticipated the cloud covered turning point, briefed the transition to timed navigation before reaching it and turned exactly at the completion of the leg time. The following leg was flown on the planned heading and the visual navigation was resumed at the first feature that became available. The interruption of the visual navigation produced negligible error.
texts.marginal: SP turned at the completion of the leg time as required, but the decision to abandon the visual search was taken only in the last seconds before the leg time expired. The trend is a late acceptance of timing as the primary reference when the feature is not visible. SP is expected to decide on the timed turn as soon as the turning point is assessed as obscured, rather than at the expiry of the leg time.

texts.0: SP, due to a clock that was never started at the departure point of the leg, did not monitor or control the determined leg durations. SP was unable to state the elapsed or remaining time on any leg and had no groundspeed figure with which to assess the navigation. IP had to run the timing for the remainder of the route and pass the required airspeed corrections.
texts.1: SP, due to leg timings written on the chart but not compared with the clock in flight, monitored the leg durations only when asked. SP produced the elapsed time and the required correction each time after IP requested it, and no independent check was made between prompts. Control of the leg durations existed only through that repeated questioning.
texts.2: SP, due to a groundspeed check omitted at the first half-leg checkpoint, initially had no assessment of the developing timing error. SP reinstated the check at the following checkpoint, computed the groundspeed against the elapsed time and adjusted the airspeed to restore the planned leg duration. Timing control was recovered without any IP input.
texts.3: SP monitored and controlled the determined durations of each leg, starting and stopping the timing at the correct points and checking groundspeed at the planned checkpoints. Airspeed corrections were computed from the elapsed time and applied while the errors were still small. Every leg was completed within the planned duration.
texts.4: SP maintained a continuous picture of elapsed time, remaining time and groundspeed for every leg and could state all three on request at any point of the route. Corrections were computed in advance of the checkpoints and applied smoothly, so no leg duration required a late adjustment. Control of the leg timings was precise throughout the navigation.
texts.marginal: SP monitored the leg durations within standards, but the timing was checked only at the turning points and no intermediate groundspeed check was made. The trend is a timing error that becomes known only when the leg is already complete and can no longer be corrected within that leg. SP is expected to check groundspeed at the half-leg checkpoint so that corrections are applied inside the leg concerned.

error_modes.label: COCKPIT WORKLOAD AND CHART MANAGEMENT DURING NAVIGATION

texts.0: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated map reading, timing and radio work inside the turn, did not sustain the navigation task. The chart was folded incorrectly for the leg in use, SP lost the position on it during the second turn and the aircraft altitude and heading were left unmonitored while SP searched the chart. IP had to take control of the aircraft while SP reorganized the cockpit.
texts.1: SP, due to workload management that left the chart and the leg data unprepared before the turning point, fell behind the aircraft on the busier legs. SP completed the map reading and the timing only after IP prompted each task in turn, and the aircraft heading drifted while SP worked head down. Recovery of the navigation task on each leg depended on that prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to an attempt to complete the position report and the chart update at the same moment, initially fell behind on the third leg and allowed the heading to drift by about 10 degrees. SP shed the secondary task, restored the heading and altitude, then completed the chart work once the aircraft was stable. The remaining legs were flown with the tasks correctly sequenced and without IP assistance.
texts.3: SP managed the cockpit workload so that map reading, timing and radio calls were sequenced without interrupting the control of the aircraft. The chart was prepared for the next leg before each turning point and the aircraft heading and altitude were maintained throughout the head down work. Navigation and aircraft control were both sustained without prompting.
texts.4: SP organized the cockpit so that every leg was set up in advance, with the chart, the heading and the leg time ready before the turning point was reached. Aircraft control, lookout and navigation tasks were interleaved smoothly even on the shortest legs, and spare capacity remained available for the radio work. No task was ever left uncompleted or performed at the wrong moment.
texts.marginal: SP managed the navigation workload within standards, but the chart and the next leg data were prepared only after the turn was completed. The trend is a cockpit that catches up with the aircraft at the start of each leg instead of being set up before the turning point. SP is expected to prepare the next leg while still inbound so that head down time after the turn is minimized.

error_modes.label: GROUND TO MAP READING INSTEAD OF THE CLOCK-MAP-GROUND METHOD

texts.0: SP, due to reading ground to map instead of applying the Clock-Map-Ground method, did not identify the preselected checkpoints of the route. SP selected prominent objects seen outside and then searched the chart for something resembling them, which produced a false fix on the second leg. The turning points that followed were passed more than 3 NM abeam and the arrival times were more than 60 seconds in error. IP had to state the actual position and direct SP back onto the planned track.
texts.1: SP, due to a chart read from the ground to the map rather than from the clock to the map and then to the ground, identified the checkpoints only after seeing them. SP passed the turning points about 2 NM abeam and about 60 seconds off the planned arrival times, at the limit of the standard, and accepted the correct feature each time only after IP named it. The same reversed sequence was used on every leg of the route.
texts.2: SP, due to an attempt on the first leg to match an isolated ground object to the chart before checking the timing, initially built a position error of about 1.5 NM and about 45 seconds. SP reverted to the Clock-Map-Ground sequence, checked the elapsed time, located the expected position on the chart and then looked outside for the matching feature. The remaining checkpoints were identified in the correct order without IP assistance.
texts.3: SP applied the Clock-Map-Ground method throughout, checking the timing, finding the corresponding location on the chart and only then looking outside for the matching feature. The chart was kept aligned with the actual track of the aircraft, so the checkpoints appeared where they were expected. Turning points were overflown within 1 NM and the arrival times were held within 30 seconds.
texts.4: SP worked from the clock to the chart to the ground on every leg, with the chart aligned in the same relative direction as the actual track. Each checkpoint was located on the chart before it became visible and was then confirmed outside without any search. Positional and timing errors along the route remained negligible.
texts.marginal: SP identified the checkpoints within standards, but the timing was consulted only after a ground feature had already attracted attention. The trend is a sequence that starts outside the cockpit and uses the chart only for confirmation, which will produce a false fix as soon as two similar features exist on the leg. SP is expected to start every identification from the clock, then the chart, and only then the ground.

error_modes.label: CROSSCHECK LIMITED TO REFERENCES OFF THE NOSE

texts.0: SP, due to crosschecking the navigation with only references off the nose of the aircraft, did not recognize turning points that lay off to one side of the track. SP never noted the relationship of the landmarks to one another, so a town of similar size on the wrong side of the leg was accepted as the turning point. The aircraft was flown more than 3 NM from the correct point and arrived more than 60 seconds off the planned time before IP identified the error and took over the navigation.
texts.1: SP, due to a visual scan confined to the sector ahead of the aircraft, recognized the turning points only when they appeared on the nose. SP passed two points about 2 NM abeam and about 60 seconds off the planned times, and located the correct feature each time after IP pointed to the confirming landmarks abeam of the track. The scan remained restricted to the nose sector for the rest of the route.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial crosscheck limited to the features straight ahead, was unable to separate two similar towns on the third leg and allowed the error to reach about 1.5 NM and about 45 seconds. SP extended the scan to each side, used the towers lying east of one of the towns to identify the correct checkpoint and regained the planned track. The remaining legs were crosschecked with references on both sides without IP input.
texts.3: SP crosschecked the navigation with references in every direction and not only off the nose of the aircraft. The arrangement of the landmarks relative to one another was used to confirm each checkpoint, so no similar feature was mistaken for the turning point. Turning points were overflown within 1 NM and within 30 seconds of the planned times.
texts.4: SP scanned as far as could be seen in each direction and used the relationship between the landmarks as the primary means of confirming every checkpoint. Features abeam and behind the track were used to keep the position continuously verified, so no identification depended on a single object ahead. Deviations from the turning points and from the planned times remained negligible.
texts.marginal: SP crosschecked the navigation within standards, but the confirming features used were almost always ahead of the aircraft and the ones abeam were noted only when the point ahead was in doubt. The trend is a scan that narrows toward the nose as the workload of the leg increases. SP is expected to include references in each direction and to use the arrangement of the landmarks relative to one another on every leg.

error_modes.label: LATE START OF TURN POINT IDENTIFICATION - NO VERIFICATION WITH MULTIPLE FEATURES
error_modes.source: technique:8.19.6.d(7)-(8) IDENTIFY TURN POINTS AND CHECKPOINT PROCEDURES (6 Ts)

texts.0: SP, due to starting the identification of the turn points only when they were expected to be overhead instead of about one to one and a half minutes out, did not recognize them in time to turn. SP had no checkpoint identified ahead of the aircraft and accepted a single feature without verifying it with any other, which produced a turn at a point more than 3 NM from the planned one and more than 60 seconds late. IP had to identify the turn point and command the turn.
texts.1: SP, due to a search for the turn point that began well inside the one to one and a half minute lead time, identified each point only as it passed under the nose. SP turned about 2 NM from the planned point and about 60 seconds off the planned time, at the limit of the standard, and the identification was confirmed only when IP called the feature. No point was verified with multiple features at any stage of the route.
texts.2: SP, due to the checkpoints of the second leg not being picked up two to five minutes ahead, started the identification late and initially reached about 1.5 NM and about 45 seconds of error. SP restored the lead time on the following leg, had the turn point identified about one minute out and verified it against a second feature before the turn. The remaining points were identified in good time without IP assistance.
texts.3: SP started trying to identify each turn point about one to one and a half minutes out and verified it with more than one feature before turning. Checkpoints were picked up two to five minutes ahead and were positively identified by one minute out. Every turn point was overflown within 1 NM and within 30 seconds of the planned time.
texts.4: SP had every checkpoint located two to five minutes ahead and positively identified well before the one minute point, each one confirmed by at least two independent features. The turn point was therefore already known and the turn was flown as a planned action rather than a reaction. Deviations from the points and from the planned times were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP identified the turn points within standards, but the search began closer to one minute than to one and a half minutes out and the verification rested on a single feature. The trend is an identification that leaves no margin to resolve a doubtful point before the turn is due. SP is expected to start looking for the turn point at the full lead time and to confirm it with multiple features.

error_modes.label: INCOMPLETE 6 Ts OVER THE CHECKPOINT
error_modes.source: technique:8.19.6.d(7)-(8) IDENTIFY TURN POINTS AND CHECKPOINT PROCEDURES (6 Ts)

texts.0: SP, due to omitting most of the 6 Ts over the positively identified checkpoint, did not establish the next leg correctly. SP neither noted the time nor adjusted the torque to the new airspeed and left the heading bug on the previous figure, so the following leg was flown at the wrong speed and without any timing reference. The next turning point was reached more than 60 seconds off the planned time and more than 3 NM from the planned position, and IP had to reconstruct the leg data.
texts.1: SP, due to a 6 Ts flow interrupted after Time and Turn, did not complete Throttle and Twist over the checkpoints. SP flew the following legs with the torque still set for the previous airspeed and reached the turning points about 60 seconds off the planned times, correcting the setting each time only after IP asked what airspeed was required. The same items were omitted at each subsequent checkpoint.
texts.2: SP, due to the Throttle item being deferred while the position report was completed, initially allowed the second leg to run about 45 seconds behind and about 1.5 NM off the planned track. SP completed the remaining Ts as soon as the radio call was finished, reset the torque for the planned airspeed and recovered the leg timing before the next turning point. The 6 Ts were completed in full at every later checkpoint without IP input.
texts.3: SP flew directly over each positively identified checkpoint and performed the 6 Ts in sequence, noting the time, turning to the new heading, adjusting the torque to the new airspeed, twisting the heading bug, tracking the course centerline at the desired altitude and making the required call. Each leg therefore began with the correct speed, heading reference and timing. Turning points were made within 1 NM and within 30 seconds.
texts.4: SP completed the 6 Ts over every checkpoint without omission and without interrupting the control of the aircraft, with a landmark off the nose selected for heading control immediately after the turn. Altitude was checked against the VFR cruising procedure and adjusted before the checkpoint, so the next leg was commenced fully set up. Timing and track errors on the following legs were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP performed the 6 Ts within standards, but the Twist and Talk items were consistently completed a good distance after the checkpoint. The trend is a flow that is started over the point and finished during the following leg, leaving the heading bug and the frequency behind the aircraft. SP is expected to complete all six items over the checkpoint so that the new leg begins with every reference already set.

error_modes.label: NO VISUAL ROLLOUT REFERENCE - CLEARING IN THE LOW ALTITUDE TURN
error_modes.source: technique:8.19.6.d(7)-(8) IDENTIFY TURN POINTS AND CHECKPOINT PROCEDURES (6 Ts)

texts.0: SP, due to turning at the checkpoint without clearing in the direction of the turn and without selecting a visual rollout reference, flew the turn entirely head down on the heading indicator. Clearing and aircraft control were not maintained during the low altitude turn and SP rolled out more than 3 NM displaced from the planned track and more than 60 seconds off the planned time for the next point. IP had to take control to clear the turn and to reestablish the aircraft on the new leg.
texts.1: SP, due to a turn commenced without a visual rollout reference having been selected outside, chased the heading indicator through the turn at low altitude. SP rolled out displaced about 2 NM from the planned track and arrived about 60 seconds off at the next point, and cleared the turn only after IP directed the lookout. The reference was again not selected at the following turning points.
texts.2: SP, due to a rollout reference chosen only after the bank was established, initially rolled out with the aircraft about 1.5 NM off the planned track and about 45 seconds behind. SP identified a suitable ground reference on the new heading, fine tuned the heading onto it and regained the planned track within the leg. Later turns were cleared and flown to a preselected visual reference without IP input.
texts.3: SP cleared in the direction of each turn, selected a visual rollout reference before rolling in and turned to that reference before fine tuning the heading. Attention remained outside the cockpit during the low altitude turns and aircraft control was maintained throughout. Rollouts placed the aircraft within 1 NM of the planned track and within 30 seconds of the planned times.
texts.4: SP selected the visual rollout reference while still inbound to each checkpoint, cleared the turn thoroughly and flew the turn to that reference with the heading indicator used only for the final fine tuning. Clearing and aircraft control at low altitude were never degraded by the navigation work. Track and timing errors after each rollout were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP flew the turns within standards, but the visual rollout reference was selected during the turn rather than before it and the clearing in the direction of the turn was brief. The trend is a turn that relies on the heading indicator at exactly the altitude where lookout matters most. SP is expected to clear the turn and pick the rollout reference before rolling in, then fine tune the heading after rollout.

error_modes.label: HEADING CORRECTION BASED ON AN UNCERTAIN LANDMARK

texts.0: SP, due to using an uncertain landmark as the basis for a heading correction, turned the aircraft away from the planned track. SP accepted a small lake among several similar ones as a positive fix and altered heading toward the assumed turning point, and the resulting track error exceeded 3 NM with an arrival more than 60 seconds off the planned time. IP had to cancel the correction, fix the position on a positive landmark and reestablish the navigation.
texts.1: SP, due to a heading correction computed from a farm and an isolated tower rather than from a positive landmark, displaced the aircraft from the planned track. SP passed the next turning point about 2 NM abeam and about 60 seconds off the planned time and reverted to the planned heading only after IP questioned the basis of the correction. Uncertain features continued to be treated as fixes on the following legs.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial correction applied on the strength of a small lake that had not been positively identified, drifted about 1.5 NM off the planned track and about 45 seconds behind. SP recognized that the feature was an uncertain landmark, removed the correction and waited for the positively identifiable bend in the road before adjusting the heading again. The remaining corrections were based on positive or linear landmarks without IP assistance.
texts.3: SP based every heading correction on positive or linear landmarks and used uncertain features only as an indication of a likely position from which the following landmarks could be anticipated. No correction was applied on the strength of a feature that could not be positively identified. Turning points were overflown within 1 NM and within 30 seconds of the planned times.
texts.4: SP classified the landmarks along the route as positive, linear or uncertain during the planning and applied that classification rigorously in flight. Corrections were computed only from positively identified features, while the uncertain ones were used solely to anticipate what should appear next. Track and timing errors remained negligible for the whole route.
texts.marginal: SP corrected the heading within standards, but on two occasions the correction was applied on an uncertain landmark and only afterwards confirmed by a positive one. The trend is an acceptance of a probable fix as the basis for a heading change. SP is expected to use uncertain landmarks only to anticipate future landmarks and to correct heading only from positively identified features.

error_modes.label: IDENTIFICATION FROM CULTURAL FEATURES - ROAD COUNTING AND CITY OUTLINE
error_modes.source: technique:8.17 CULTURAL FEATURES (Roads, Bridges, Railroads, Power Lines, Populated Areas, Coastal Hydrography)

texts.0: SP, due to counting roads as an orientation technique and identifying a populated area from its charted outline alone, fixed the aircraft over the wrong town. The roads seen did not match the charted classification, as only dual lane highways are reliably portrayed, and the built up area had grown well beyond the outline on the chart. SP turned on a false fix, missed the turning point by more than 3 NM and arrived more than 60 seconds off the planned time, and IP had to reestablish the position.
texts.1: SP, due to reliance on the charted road classification for two lane roads, identified the turning point on a road that resembled the one on the chart but was not it. SP passed the point about 2 NM abeam and about 60 seconds off the planned time and accepted the correct feature only when IP described the unique element that differentiated the town. The same reliance on the charted appearance of the roads persisted on the following legs.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial attempt to identify the third checkpoint by counting the roads crossing the leg, hesitated over two similar towns and allowed the error to reach about 1.5 NM and about 45 seconds. SP stopped counting roads, identified the town by a unique element that differentiated it from the other one and confirmed the road by its planned time of arrival. The remaining checkpoints were identified from distinguishing elements without IP input.
texts.3: SP identified the cultural features by the elements that differentiate them rather than by counting roads or by the charted city outline, and used bridges and coastlines as position and time checks once positively identified. Roads that were seen but hard to classify were resolved by their planned time of arrival. Turning points were overflown within 1 NM and within 30 seconds of the planned times.
texts.4: SP treated each populated area as identifiable only by a unique differentiating element and expected the actual extent of the towns to differ from the charted outlines. Bridges over the double line streams and the coastline were used as positive fixes and time checks exactly as planned, and no attempt was made to orient by counting roads. Position and timing errors along the route remained negligible.
texts.marginal: SP identified the cultural features within standards, but the first assessment of each town was still made from its charted shape and only then confirmed by a differentiating element. The trend is an expectation that the ground will look like the chart, which will fail at the first town that has grown beyond its charted outline. SP is expected to identify populated areas from a unique element and to treat the charted road classification as unreliable except for dual lane highways.

error_modes.label: ANXIETY DISORIENTATION AFTER A MISSING LANDMARK

texts.0: SP, due to anxiety disorientation after the chart to ground method failed to produce an anticipated landmark, treated the missing feature as proof of being lost while the aircraft was still on course. SP abandoned the planned headings and times and wandered while deciding what to do, without checking the clock or reviewing the progress from the last known position. The route error grew beyond 3 NM and beyond 60 seconds and IP had to take over the navigation and restore the aircraft to the planned track.
texts.1: SP, due to the same anxiety after an expected landmark did not appear, began to search away from the planned heading instead of continuing on the preplanned heading and time. SP reached the next turning point about 2 NM abeam and about 60 seconds off the planned time and resumed the planned navigation only after IP directed the return to the briefed heading. The reaction to a missing feature was unchanged on the following leg.
texts.2: SP, due to a brief loss of confidence when an anticipated landmark was not seen, initially deviated from the planned heading and allowed the error to reach about 1.5 NM and about 45 seconds. SP checked the clock, noted the time, reviewed the progress from the last known position and elected to continue on the preplanned headings and times until the next positive landmark appeared. The navigation was recovered without any IP intervention.
texts.3: SP continued flying the preplanned headings and times when an anticipated landmark failed to appear, recognizing that a missing feature is not by itself evidence of being lost. The clock was checked immediately and the progress from the last known position was reviewed while the aircraft remained on the planned track. The following turning point was made within 1 NM and within 30 seconds of the planned time.
texts.4: SP remained composed when an expected feature did not appear, noted the time at once, reviewed the extent of the doubt against the last known position and continued the preplanned headings and times without any deviation. The position was reconfirmed at the next positive landmark and the fuel state was checked against the minimum required to complete the route. The episode produced negligible effect on the track and on the timing of the navigation.
texts.marginal: SP handled the missing landmark within standards, but the immediate reaction was a widening visual search and a small heading deviation before the preplanned heading was resumed. The trend is a doubt that translates into aircraft movement before the clock and the last known position have been consulted. SP is expected to check the clock first, keep flying the preplanned headings and times and avoid maneuvering while deciding what to do.
